c: King Nebuchadnezzar II reigned over Babylon from 605 to 562
. He secured and extended the empire of his father, Nabopolassar (626–605
). Beyond the scriptural record, many ancient Babylonian documents report Nebuchadnezzar’s accomplishments.
, Babylon, like Judah, was under the domination of Assyria, but in that year Nabopolassar began a revolt that would change the world. In 612
, the Babylonians captured Nineveh, Assyria’s capital, and again defeated the Assyrians at Haran in 609
. By the time of this battle, Nabopolassar’s son Nebuchadnezzar played a leading role in the army. In 605

, Nebuchadnezzar defeated the remnant of the Assyrian army at Carchemish; this victory also pushed the Egyptians back within their borders. In the same year, Nabopolassar died and his son became king.
Following his victory at Carchemish in 605
, Nebuchadnezzar conquered Syria and surrounding areas, including Judah. In that year, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem for the first time (
). He took away a number of the Temple vessels and some of the leading young citizens of Judah, including Daniel and his three friends. Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem again in 597
and destroyed the city and Temple in 586
, exiling most of the remaining people (

A detailed and interesting personal description of Nebuchadnezzar is found in Daniel. He brought Daniel and his friends to Babylon in order to educate them in the ways of Babylonia, but God used Daniel to teach Nebuchadnezzar about himself. After being humbled for his great pride (
), Nebuchadnezzar acknowledged the Lord’s sovereignty and power (
), though he probably never worshiped the true God exclusively.

This section contains stories and dreams from the experiences of Daniel and his friends in Babylon. Daniel exercised his special gift of understanding the meaning of dreams and his mastery of literature and science (
